items.stem: Which pair of bases are both purines?
items.answer: adenine and guanine
items.markingKey: C. Purines (A, G) have two rings.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "A nucleotide is made of a sugar, a base and an amino acid." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base; amino acids are the monomers of proteins.
items.markingKey: A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base; amino acids are the monomers of proteins. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the 3′ end of a polynucleotide strand and the 5′ end.
items.answer: The 5′ end terminates with a phosphate attached to carbon 5′ of the sugar; the 3′ end terminates with a free hydroxyl group on carbon 3′.
items.markingKey: The 5′ end terminates with a phosphate attached to carbon 5′ of the sugar; the 3′ end terminates with a free hydroxyl group on carbon 3′. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray diffraction image “Photograph 51” (1952) as an example, explain how evidence was used to build the model of DNA structure.
items.answer: The X-shaped pattern revealed a helix with a regular repeat and the phosphate groups on the outside. Watson and Crick combined this evidence with Chargaff’s ratios and model building to propose a double helix with complementary base pairs – an example of models being built from several lines of evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (The X-shaped pattern revealed a helix with a regular repeat and the phosphate groups on the outside.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Watson and Crick combined this evidence with Chargaff’s ratios and model building to propose a double helix with complementary base pairs – an example of models being built from several lines of evidence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how evidence was used to build the model of DNA structure.

items.stem: A synthetic double-stranded DNA fragment contains the strand 5′-GCAGATCATATATAC-3′ paired with its complement. How many hydrogen bonds join the two strands? Calculate also the percentage of G–C base pairs and predict how this fragment would compare in melting temperature with a fragment of equal length containing 25 % G–C.
items.answer: 35 hydrogen bonds; 33 % G–C; higher melting temperature
items.markingKey: 10 A–T pairs × 2 + 5 G–C pairs × 3 = 35 (M1 A1); 5/15 × 100 = 33 % (A1); more G–C = more hydrogen bonds = higher melting temperature (R1).

items.stem: A student’s model of DNA shows both strands with their 5′ ends at the top. What is wrong with the model?
options: The bases should be on the outside.
The strands should be antiparallel, with one 5′ end at the top and one at the bottom.
The 3′ ends should both be at the top.
items.answer: The strands should be antiparallel, with one 5′ end at the top and one at the bottom.
items.markingKey: B. DNA strands are antiparallel.

items.stem: Describe the structure of DNA, including how the two strands are held together and how the structure allows replication.
items.answer: Nucleotides: deoxyribose, phosphate, base; covalent sugar–phosphate backbone; two strands antiparallel; double helix; bases inside; A–T (2 H bonds), G–C (3 H bonds); purine with pyrimidine; complementary pairing means each strand is a template; hydrogen bonds easily broken for separation; sequence of bases stores information.
items.markingKey: Nucleotides: deoxyribose, phosphate, base; covalent sugar–phosphate backbone; two strands antiparallel; double helix; bases inside; A–T (2 H bonds), G–C (3 H bonds); purine with pyrimidine; complementary pairing means each strand is a template; hydrogen bonds easily broken for separation; sequence of bases stores information.

items.stem: "Watson and Crick deserve the main credit for discovering the structure of DNA." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Scientific discoveries are collaborative; Watson and Crick made the decisive synthesis, but Franklin, Wilkins and Chargaff provided essential evidence, so credit should be shared.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they built the first model consistent with all available evidence and proposed a copying mechanism; their insight into complementary base pairing was original. Arguments against: their model relied on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data, used without her full knowledge; Chargaff’s base ratios and the work of Wilkins were essential. Supported judgement: Scientific discoveries are collaborative; Watson and Crick made the decisive synthesis, but Franklin, Wilkins and Chargaff provided essential evidence, so credit should be shared. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "sugar–phosphate backbone".
items.answer: The chain of alternating pentose sugars and phosphate groups linked by covalent (phosphodiester) bonds that forms the outside of each strand of a nucleic acid
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the chain of alternating pentose sugars and phosphate groups linked by covalent (phosphodiester) bonds that forms the outside of each strand of a nucleic acid. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a nucleotide allows nucleotides to be linked into a polymer.
items.answer: The phosphate on C5′ of one nucleotide forms a covalent bond (by condensation) with the –OH on C3′ of the sugar of the next; repeated linkage forms a sugar–phosphate backbone with bases projecting from it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The phosphate on C5′ of one nucleotide forms a covalent bond (by condensation) with the –OH on C3′ of the sugar of the next; repeated linkage forms a sugar–phosphate backbone with bases projecting from it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which feature of DNA structure makes it chemically stable enough to store information for long periods?
options: covalently bonded sugar–phosphate backbones with bases protected inside the helix
items.answer: covalently bonded sugar–phosphate backbones with bases protected inside the helix
items.markingKey: D. The backbone is covalently bonded; bases are stacked inside.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of DNA makes it suitable for storing genetic information.
items.answer: The sequence of bases along a strand can vary without restriction and carries the information; the double helix with covalent backbones is stable; complementary base pairing allows accurate copying and repair using one strand as a template.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The sequence of bases along a strand can vary without restriction and carries the information; the double helix with covalent backbones is stable; complementary base pairing allows accurate copying and repair using one strand as a template. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Draw a simple diagram of a section of DNA showing four nucleotides in two antiparallel strands. Outline the features it must show.
items.answer: Two strands each of two nucleotides; sugar–phosphate backbones; bases paired A–T and C–G by hydrogen bonds (dashed); strands labelled 5′ and 3′ at opposite ends.
items.markingKey: Two strands each of two nucleotides; sugar–phosphate backbones; bases paired A–T and C–G by hydrogen bonds (dashed); strands labelled 5′ and 3′ at opposite ends.

items.stem:
In the Hershey–Chase experiment, E. coli infected with radioactively labelled T2 phage were agitated in a blender for different times. The percentage of each isotope released into the supernatant and the percentage of bacteria still infected were measured.

Blending time / min | ³⁵S released / % | ³²P released / %
0 | 0 | 0
1 | 47 | 13
2 | 67 | 19
4 | 79 | 23
6 | 82 | 22
8 | 81 | 23

After 8 minutes 96 % of bacteria were still infected.

(a) State the percentage of ³⁵S released after 4 minutes of blending. [1]
(b) Compare the release of ³⁵S and ³²P during blending. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference between the percentages of ³⁵S and ³²P remaining with the bacteria after 8 minutes. [2]
items.answer: (a) 79 % (b) Both rise quickly in the first 2 minutes and then level off; far more ³⁵S (about 81 %) than ³²P (about 23 %) is released. (c) 58 percentage points
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 79 % (A1). (b) [2] Both increase then plateau (A1); ³⁵S release much greater than ³²P at each time (A1). (c) [2] ³²P remaining 77 %, ³⁵S remaining 19 % (M1); difference 58 (A1).

items.stem:
In the late 1940s Erwin Chargaff analysed the base composition of DNA from many organisms. Some of his results (percentage of each base) are shown.

Source of DNA | A | G | C | T
salmon (Salmo salar) | 29.7 | 20.8 | 20.4 | 29.1
human (Homo sapiens) | 30.9 | 19.9 | 19.8 | 29.4
Escherichia coli | 24.7 | 26.0 | 25.7 | 23.6
wheat (Triticum aestivum) | 27.3 | 22.7 | 22.8 | 27.1

(a) Calculate the ratio of A to T and of G to C for wheat (Triticum aestivum). [2]
(b) Calculate the ratio of purines to pyrimidines, (A + G)/(C + T), for wheat (Triticum aestivum). [2]
(c) Identify the organism in the table whose DNA has the highest proportion of G + C. [1]
(d) Explain how these data support the model of DNA proposed by Watson and Crick. [3]
items.answer: (a) A/T = 1.01; G/C = 1.00 (b) 1.00 (c) Escherichia coli (51.7 %) (d) A ≈ T and G ≈ C in each species, consistent with complementary base pairing of A with T and G with C in a double-stranded molecule; purine/pyrimidine ≈ 1 fits one purine pairing with one pyrimidine.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 27.3/27.1 = 1.01 (A1); 22.7/22.8 = 1.00 (A1). (b) [2] (27.3 + 22.7)/(22.8 + 27.1) (M1) = 1.00 (A1). (c) [1] Escherichia coli (A1). (d) [3] A ≈ T and G ≈ C (A1); complementary base pairing (R1); purine with pyrimidine / ratio ≈ 1 (R1).

items.stem:
In the late 1940s Erwin Chargaff analysed the base composition of DNA from many organisms. Some of his results (percentage of each base) are shown.

Source of DNA | A | G | C | T
yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) | 31.3 | 18.7 | 17.1 | 32.9
sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus) | 32.8 | 17.7 | 17.3 | 32.1
chicken (Gallus gallus) | 28.0 | 22.0 | 21.6 | 28.4
octopus (Octopus vulgaris) | 33.2 | 17.6 | 17.6 | 31.6

(a) Calculate the ratio of A to T and of G to C for sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus). [2]
(b) Calculate the ratio of purines to pyrimidines, (A + G)/(C + T), for sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus). [2]
(c) Identify the organism in the table whose DNA has the highest proportion of G + C. [1]
(d) Explain how these data support the model of DNA proposed by Watson and Crick. [3]
items.answer: (a) A/T = 1.02; G/C = 1.02 (b) 1.02 (c) chicken (Gallus gallus) (43.6 %) (d) A ≈ T and G ≈ C in each species, consistent with complementary base pairing of A with T and G with C in a double-stranded molecule; purine/pyrimidine ≈ 1 fits one purine pairing with one pyrimidine.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 32.8/32.1 = 1.02 (A1); 17.7/17.3 = 1.02 (A1). (b) [2] (32.8 + 17.7)/(17.3 + 32.1) (M1) = 1.02 (A1). (c) [1] chicken (Gallus gallus) (A1). (d) [3] A ≈ T and G ≈ C (A1); complementary base pairing (R1); purine with pyrimidine / ratio ≈ 1 (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "genome"?
options: The whole of the genetic information of an organism
The pentose sugar in RNA nucleotides, which has a hydroxyl group on carbon 2′
A single-stranded RNA copy of a gene that carries the coded information to ribosomes for translation
A nitrogenous base with a single-ring structure (cytosine, thymine or uracil)
items.answer: The whole of the genetic information of an organism
items.markingKey: A. "genome" is the whole of the genetic information of an organism.

items.stem: Which explains why A pairs with T rather than with C?
options: A and T are the same size.
A and C are both pyrimidines.
The shapes and positions of hydrogen-bonding groups match only for A–T and G–C.
A–C pairs would be too narrow for the helix.
items.answer: The shapes and positions of hydrogen-bonding groups match only for A–T and G–C.
items.markingKey: C. Specific hydrogen-bonding geometry determines pairing.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the base pairing between DNA and RNA and the base pairing of DNA.
items.answer: In DNA adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine; when RNA pairs with DNA (or RNA with RNA) adenine pairs with uracil instead of thymine.
items.markingKey: In DNA adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine; when RNA pairs with DNA (or RNA with RNA) adenine pairs with uracil instead of thymine. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the production of human insulin by genetically modified Escherichia coli as an example, explain the universality of the genetic code and base sequence as information.
items.answer: The human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, which produced functional human insulin. Bacteria read the same codons as human cells, so the human base sequence is translated into the same amino acid sequence.
items.markingKey: Context (The human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, which produced functional human insulin.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Bacteria read the same codons as human cells, so the human base sequence is translated into the same amino acid sequence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the universality of the genetic code and base sequence as information.

items.stem: Which sequence is complementary to 5′-GCCATA-3′, written 5′→3′?
items.answer: 5′-TATGGC-3′
items.markingKey: A. Complement 3′-CGGTAT-5′ read 5′→3′ = TATGGC.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The base sequence of DNA alone determines all the characteristics of an organism."
items.answer: Base sequence provides the information, but the phenotype results from its interaction with gene regulation and the environment, so it does not alone determine all characteristics.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the base sequence encodes proteins and functional RNAs that build and run the organism; mutations that change base sequences can change characteristics. Arguments against: environmental factors and epigenetic modifications affect gene expression; identical twins with the same sequence can differ in characteristics. Supported judgement: Base sequence provides the information, but the phenotype results from its interaction with gene regulation and the environment, so it does not alone determine all characteristics.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The order of nucleotides along a nucleic acid strand, which encodes genetic information"?
items.answer: base sequence
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of base sequence.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Adenine pairs with guanine because they are both purines." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine: adenine with thymine (or uracil) and guanine with cytosine.
items.markingKey: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine: adenine with thymine (or uracil) and guanine with cytosine. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how complementary base pairing allows DNA to act as a template.
items.answer: Because A pairs only with T and G only with C, the sequence of one strand specifies the sequence of the complementary strand; when the strands separate, free nucleotides pair with the exposed bases, rebuilding the sequence exactly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Because A pairs only with T and G only with C, the sequence of one strand specifies the sequence of the complementary strand; when the strands separate, free nucleotides pair with the exposed bases, rebuilding the sequence exactly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: One strand of DNA has the base sequence 5′-CACCGAGGCGTC-3′. State the base sequence of the complementary strand, written in the 3′→5′ direction.
items.answer: 3′-GTGGCTCCGCAG-5′
items.markingKey: Each base replaced by its complement (A↔T, G↔C) (M1); written 3′-GTGGCTCCGCAG-5′ (A1).

items.stem: A gene sequence is 1500 base pairs long. Assuming each position can be any of the four bases, how many different sequences of this length are possible?
items.answer: 4¹⁵⁰⁰
items.markingKey: C. 4ⁿ with n = 1500.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of DNA allows it to store and copy an almost unlimited range of genetic information.
items.answer: Four bases; unrestricted sequence = 4ⁿ possibilities; information in base sequence; complementary pairing A–T, G–C; strands separate and each acts as template; specific pairing ensures accurate copies; hydrogen bonds easy to break; covalent backbone stable.
items.markingKey: Four bases; unrestricted sequence = 4ⁿ possibilities; information in base sequence; complementary pairing A–T, G–C; strands separate and each acts as template; specific pairing ensures accurate copies; hydrogen bonds easy to break; covalent backbone stable.

items.stem: Which statement about the number of strands in DNA and RNA is generally correct?
options: DNA is double-stranded and RNA is single-stranded.
DNA is single-stranded and RNA double-stranded.
items.answer: DNA is double-stranded and RNA is single-stranded.
items.markingKey: B. Exceptions exist in some viruses.

items.stem: A student claims: "All RNA molecules are single linear strands with no structure." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: RNA is single-stranded but can fold and base-pair with itself, e.g. tRNA forms a clover-leaf shape and rRNA forms part of ribosome structure.
items.markingKey: RNA is single-stranded but can fold and base-pair with itself, e.g. tRNA forms a clover-leaf shape and rRNA forms part of ribosome structure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between DNA and RNA.
items.answer: DNA contains deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.
items.markingKey: DNA contains deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 shows the structural differences between RNA and DNA.
items.answer: Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA coding for the spike protein; cells translate it and the mRNA is soon degraded. The instability of single-stranded RNA means it does not persist or enter the nucleus, so it is translated briefly then broken down.
items.markingKey: Context (Lipid nanoparticles deliver mRNA coding for the spike protein; cells translate it and the mRNA is soon degraded.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The instability of single-stranded RNA means it does not persist or enter the nucleus, so it is translated briefly then broken down. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the structural differences between RNA and DNA.

items.stem: An analysis of a viral genome gives: A 24 %, U 31 %, G 23 %, C 22 %. What type of genome does the virus have?
items.answer: single-stranded RNA
items.markingKey: B. Uracil indicates RNA; A ≠ U indicates single-stranded.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the structure of DNA and RNA.
items.answer: Similarities: both polynucleotides; sugar–phosphate backbone; covalent bonds between nucleotides; bases A, G, C in both; complementary pairing possible. Differences: deoxyribose vs ribose; thymine vs uracil; usually double-stranded helix vs single strand; DNA longer; DNA more stable.
items.markingKey: Similarities: both polynucleotides; sugar–phosphate backbone; covalent bonds between nucleotides; bases A, G, C in both; complementary pairing possible. Differences: deoxyribose vs ribose; thymine vs uracil; usually double-stranded helix vs single strand; DNA longer; DNA more stable.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "messenger RNA (mRNA)"?
options: A usually single-stranded nucleic acid made of ribonucleotides containing the bases A, U, G and C
The order of nucleotides along a nucleic acid strand, which encodes genetic information
A single-stranded RNA copy of a gene that carries the coded information to ribosomes for translation
The pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine; it pairs with adenine
items.answer: A single-stranded RNA copy of a gene that carries the coded information to ribosomes for translation
items.markingKey: C. "messenger RNA (mRNA)" is a single-stranded RNA copy of a gene that carries the coded information to ribosomes for translation.

items.stem: Which feature is shared by DNA and RNA?
options: nucleotides linked by covalent bonds between sugar and phosphate
items.answer: nucleotides linked by covalent bonds between sugar and phosphate
items.markingKey: C. Both are polynucleotides with sugar–phosphate backbones.

items.stem: Explain why the differences in structure between DNA and RNA suit their different functions.
items.answer: DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose (more stable), thymine – suits long-term, protected storage and accurate copying; RNA: single-stranded, ribose (less stable) – suits short-lived messenger roles, can fold into shapes (tRNA, rRNA) and be broken down quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose (more stable), thymine – suits long-term, protected storage and accurate copying; RNA: single-stranded, ribose (less stable) – suits short-lived messenger roles, can fold into shapes (tRNA, rRNA) and be broken down quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
In the Hershey–Chase experiment, E. coli infected with radioactively labelled T2 phage were agitated in a blender for different times. The percentage of each isotope released into the supernatant and the percentage of bacteria still infected were measured.

Blending time / min | ³⁵S released / % | ³²P released / %
0 | 0 | 0
1 | 47 | 13
2 | 65 | 18
4 | 79 | 21
6 | 79 | 22
8 | 84 | 23

After 8 minutes 98 % of bacteria were still infected.

(a) State the percentage of ³⁵S released after 4 minutes of blending. [1]
(b) Compare the release of ³⁵S and ³²P during blending. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference between the percentages of ³⁵S and ³²P remaining with the bacteria after 8 minutes. [2]
items.answer: (a) 79 % (b) Both rise quickly in the first 2 minutes and then level off; far more ³⁵S (about 84 %) than ³²P (about 23 %) is released. (c) 61 percentage points
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 79 % (A1). (b) [2] Both increase then plateau (A1); ³⁵S release much greater than ³²P at each time (A1). (c) [2] ³²P remaining 77 %, ³⁵S remaining 16 % (M1); difference 61 (A1).

items.stem: "RNA contains thymine and deoxyribose, just like DNA." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine and ribose instead of deoxyribose.
items.markingKey: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine and ribose instead of deoxyribose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "RNA, rather than DNA, was the genetic material of the first living cells." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The RNA world hypothesis is strongly supported by ribozymes and modern cell biology, but direct evidence is lacking; it remains the best current hypothesis rather than an established fact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions (ribozymes); ribose is produced more easily than deoxyribose in prebiotic chemistry experiments. Arguments against: RNA is unstable and would degrade quickly; there is no direct fossil evidence of an RNA world. Supported judgement: The RNA world hypothesis is strongly supported by ribozymes and modern cell biology, but direct evidence is lacking; it remains the best current hypothesis rather than an established fact. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The observation that in double-stranded DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine"?
items.answer: Chargaff’s rules
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Chargaff’s rules.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the ³²P batch and the ³⁵S batch in the Hershey–Chase experiment.
items.answer: In the ³²P batch the DNA was labelled and most radioactivity was found in the pellet (inside bacteria); in the ³⁵S batch the protein coat was labelled and most radioactivity remained in the supernatant (outside bacteria).
items.markingKey: In the ³²P batch the DNA was labelled and most radioactivity was found in the pellet (inside bacteria); in the ³⁵S batch the protein coat was labelled and most radioactivity remained in the supernatant (outside bacteria). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In double-stranded DNA from a species, 18 % of the bases are guanine. What percentage are adenine?
Sana writes: "Chargaff’s rules apply to all nucleic acids." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The A = T and G = C ratios apply to double-stranded DNA; single-stranded DNA or RNA genomes need not follow them.
items.markingKey: The A = T and G = C ratios apply to double-stranded DNA; single-stranded DNA or RNA genomes need not follow them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe the Hershey–Chase experiment and explain how its results, together with Chargaff’s data, contributed to understanding of the nature of the genetic material.
items.answer: Two batches of T2 phage: ³⁵S labels protein, ³²P labels DNA; infect E. coli; blend to remove coats; centrifuge – bacteria in pellet; ³²P in pellet, ³⁵S in supernatant; DNA enters cell, directs phage production. Chargaff: base composition varies between species – falsifies tetranucleotide hypothesis – DNA can carry information; A = T, G = C – supported complementary base pairing in Watson–Crick model.
items.markingKey: Two batches of T2 phage: ³⁵S labels protein, ³²P labels DNA; infect E. coli; blend to remove coats; centrifuge – bacteria in pellet; ³²P in pellet, ³⁵S in supernatant; DNA enters cell, directs phage production. Chargaff: base composition varies between species – falsifies tetranucleotide hypothesis – DNA can carry information; A = T, G = C – supported complementary base pairing in Watson–Crick model.

items.stem: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, where was most ³²P found after blending and centrifugation?
options: evenly divided between pellet and supernatant
it was destroyed by the blender
in the supernatant with the phage coats
in the pellet containing the bacteria
items.answer: in the pellet containing the bacteria
items.markingKey: D. Phage DNA entered the bacteria, which sediment into the pellet.

items.stem: Chargaff found A ≈ T and G ≈ C in many species. How did this help Watson and Crick?
options: It suggested specific pairing of A with T and G with C.
It showed that DNA is single-stranded.
It showed the helix has three strands.
It proved that DNA is the genetic material.
items.answer: It suggested specific pairing of A with T and G with C.
items.markingKey: A. Equal ratios fit complementary base pairing.

items.stem: Analysis of double-stranded DNA from a marine bacterium shows that 32.1 % of the bases are cytosine. Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. Explain why this calculation would not be valid for a single-stranded viral genome.
items.answer: adenine 17.9 %, thymine 17.9 %, guanine 32.1 %; in single-stranded nucleic acid bases are not paired, so A need not equal T and G need not equal C.
items.markingKey: cytosine pairs with guanine so it is also 32.1 % (A1); remaining 35.8 % shared equally by the other pair = 17.9 % each (A1). No complementary strand in a single-stranded genome so Chargaff’s equalities need not hold (R1).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Hershey and Chase reported that after blending for several minutes about 80 % of the ³⁵S was released into the supernatant, while only about 20–35 % of the ³²P was released; most ³²P remained with the bacteria, and about 30 % of it was passed on to the next generation of phages.
— Summary of Hershey, A. D. and Chase, M. (1952) J. Gen. Physiol. 36: 39–56

Explain why these results were considered strong but not conclusive evidence that DNA is the genetic material.
items.answer: Strong: most DNA entered and some ³²P appeared in progeny; most protein stayed outside. Not conclusive: about 20 % of ³⁵S remained with bacteria, so some protein may have entered; blending was incomplete; the result was for one phage only; other evidence (Avery 1944, Chargaff) was needed.
items.markingKey: Strong: most DNA entered and some ³²P appeared in progeny; most protein stayed outside. Not conclusive: about 20 % of ³⁵S remained with bacteria, so some protein may have entered; blending was incomplete; the result was for one phage only; other evidence (Avery 1944, Chargaff) was needed. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "The Hershey–Chase experiment proved that DNA is the genetic material of all organisms." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It provided strong evidence for one phage; acceptance for all organisms relied on the convergence of several independent lines of evidence, so “proved for all organisms” overstates it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: labelled DNA entered bacteria and was associated with new phage production; the result supported earlier work by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty. Arguments against: the experiment used only one virus, so generalising to all organisms is not justified; some protein contamination occurred, so the result was not absolute. Supported judgement: It provided strong evidence for one phage; acceptance for all organisms relied on the convergence of several independent lines of evidence, so “proved for all organisms” overstates it. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "antiparallel"?
options: Describes the two strands of DNA running in opposite directions, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′
A usually single-stranded nucleic acid made of ribonucleotides containing the bases A, U, G and C
The observation that in double-stranded DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine
The pentose sugar in RNA nucleotides, which has a hydroxyl group on carbon 2′
items.answer: Describes the two strands of DNA running in opposite directions, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′
items.markingKey: A. "antiparallel" is describes the two strands of DNA running in opposite directions, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.

items.stem: Which feature of nucleic acids allows an almost limitless variety of genetic information to be stored?
options: bases pair in only one way
there is no restriction on the sequence of bases along a strand
items.answer: there is no restriction on the sequence of bases along a strand
items.markingKey: B. Any base can follow any other, so 4ⁿ sequences are possible.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine; it pairs with adenine"?
items.answer: uracil
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of uracil.

items.stem: Explain how Chargaff’s data falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis.
items.answer: The hypothesis predicted equal amounts (25 %) of each base in all DNA; Chargaff showed base composition varied between species (e.g. A 31 % in humans vs 25 % in E. coli), so DNA is not a simple repeat and could carry varied information.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The hypothesis predicted equal amounts (25 %) of each base in all DNA; Chargaff showed base composition varied between species (e.g. A 31 % in humans vs 25 % in E. coli), so DNA is not a simple repeat and could carry varied information. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In DNA the two strands are joined by covalent bonds between the bases." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent bonds join nucleotides within each strand.
items.markingKey: The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent bonds join nucleotides within each strand. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The genetic code is the sequence of bases in an individual’s DNA." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The genetic code is the set of codon-to-amino-acid rules; the base sequence is the specific information that the code is used to read.
items.markingKey: The genetic code is the set of codon-to-amino-acid rules; the base sequence is the specific information that the code is used to read. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.
items.answer: DNA contains deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.
items.markingKey: DNA contains deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why was sulfur used to label phage protein rather than phosphorus?
options: Proteins contain sulfur but DNA does not.
DNA contains sulfur but proteins do not.
Sulfur is less radioactive than phosphorus.
items.answer: Proteins contain sulfur but DNA does not.
items.markingKey: A. Each label must be specific to one type of molecule.

items.stem: Distinguish between the 5′ end and the 3′ end of a polynucleotide strand.
items.answer: The 5′ end terminates with a phosphate attached to carbon 5′ of the sugar; the 3′ end terminates with a free hydroxyl group on carbon 3′.
items.markingKey: The 5′ end terminates with a phosphate attached to carbon 5′ of the sugar; the 3′ end terminates with a free hydroxyl group on carbon 3′. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which sequence is complementary to 5′-AGCACA-3′, written 5′→3′?
items.answer: 5′-TGTGCT-3′
items.markingKey: C. Complement 3′-TCGTGT-5′ read 5′→3′ = TGTGCT.

items.stem: Using the Hershey–Chase experiment of 1952 as an example, explain the use of radioactive labelling to test a hypothesis.
items.answer: T2 phages labelled with ³²P or ³⁵S infected E. coli; after blending and centrifugation, ³²P was mainly in the bacterial pellet and ³⁵S in the supernatant. Specific labels allowed the fate of DNA and protein to be traced separately, providing evidence that DNA enters the cell and carries genetic information.

items.stem: Briefly describe Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray diffraction image “Photograph 51” (1952) and explain what it reveals about how evidence was used to build the model of DNA structure.
items.answer: The X-shaped pattern revealed a helix with a regular repeat and the phosphate groups on the outside. Watson and Crick combined this evidence with Chargaff’s ratios and model building to propose a double helix with complementary base pairs – an example of models being built from several lines of evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (The X-shaped pattern revealed a helix with a regular repeat and the phosphate groups on the outside.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A DNA strand has the sequence 5′-ATGCCA-3′. Which is the complementary strand, written 5′→3′?
items.answer: 5′-TGGCAT-3′
items.markingKey: B. Complement is 3′-TACGGT-5′; read 5′→3′ it is TGGCAT.

items.stem: Short-lived mRNA molecules are useful to a cell because
options: gene expression can be switched off quickly when the mRNA is broken down
items.answer: gene expression can be switched off quickly when the mRNA is broken down

items.stem: The DNA of virus φX174 contains A 24 %, T 31 %, G 23 %, C 22 %. What does this suggest?
items.answer: Its DNA is single-stranded.
items.markingKey: A. A ≠ T and G ≠ C, so there is no complementary second strand.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Watson and Crick deserve the main credit for discovering the structure of DNA."
items.answer: Scientific discoveries are collaborative; Watson and Crick made the decisive synthesis, but Franklin, Wilkins and Chargaff provided essential evidence, so credit should be shared.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they built the first model consistent with all available evidence and proposed a copying mechanism; their insight into complementary base pairing was original. Arguments against: their model relied on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data, used without her full knowledge; Chargaff’s base ratios and the work of Wilkins were essential. Supported judgement: Scientific discoveries are collaborative; Watson and Crick made the decisive synthesis, but Franklin, Wilkins and Chargaff provided essential evidence, so credit should be shared.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The base sequence of DNA alone determines all the characteristics of an organism."
items.answer: Base sequence provides the information, but the phenotype results from its interaction with gene regulation and the environment, so it does not alone determine all characteristics.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the base sequence encodes proteins and functional RNAs that build and run the organism; mutations that change base sequences can change characteristics. Arguments against: environmental factors and epigenetic modifications affect gene expression; identical twins with the same sequence can differ in characteristics. Supported judgement: Base sequence provides the information, but the phenotype results from its interaction with gene regulation and the environment, so it does not alone determine all characteristics. items.stem: "RNA, rather than DNA, was the genetic material of the first living cells." Discuss.
items.answer: The RNA world hypothesis is strongly supported by ribozymes and modern cell biology, but direct evidence is lacking; it remains the best current hypothesis rather than an established fact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions (ribozymes); ribose is produced more easily than deoxyribose in prebiotic chemistry experiments. Arguments against: RNA is unstable and would degrade quickly; there is no direct fossil evidence of an RNA world. items.stem:
In the Hershey–Chase experiment, E. coli infected with radioactively labelled T2 phage were agitated in a blender for different times. The percentage of each isotope released into the supernatant and the percentage of bacteria still infected were measured.

Blending time / min | ³⁵S released / % | ³²P released / %
0 | 0 | 0
1 | 43 | 12
2 | 64 | 18
4 | 74 | 22
6 | 79 | 22
8 | 76 | 23

After 8 minutes 98 % of bacteria were still infected.

(a) State the percentage of ³⁵S released after 4 minutes of blending. [1]
(b) Compare the release of ³⁵S and ³²P during blending. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference between the percentages of ³⁵S and ³²P remaining with the bacteria after 8 minutes. [2]
(d) Explain why the percentage of bacteria still infected is important in interpreting the results. [2]
(e) Explain what the results suggest about the nature of the genetic material. [3]
(f) Suggest why about 20 % of ³⁵S was never released. [1]
(g) Explain why radioactive sulfur and phosphorus were used as labels. [2]
items.answer: (a) 74 % (b) Both rise quickly in the first 2 minutes and then level off; far more ³⁵S (about 76 %) than ³²P (about 23 %) is released. (c) 53 percentage points (d) It shows that blending did not stop infection: the genetic material had already entered the cells, so the coats removed by blending (³⁵S) were not needed for infection. (e) DNA (³²P) mostly remains with/inside the bacteria while protein (³⁵S) is mostly removed; infection continues, so DNA is the material that enters and directs phage production. (f) Some coats remained attached to cells even after blending / some protein entered / incomplete separation in centrifugation. (g) Sulfur is found in proteins (some amino acids) but not DNA; phosphorus is in DNA (phosphate groups) but not in protein, so each label tracks one molecule.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 74 % (A1). (b) [2] Both increase then plateau (A1); ³⁵S release much greater than ³²P at each time (A1). (c) [2] ³²P remaining 77 %, ³⁵S remaining 24 % (M1); difference 53 (A1). (d) [2] Blending does not prevent infection (A1); so material in the supernatant (protein) is not required (R1). (e) [3] DNA enters cells (A1); protein stays outside (A1); DNA carries genetic information (R1). (f) [1] Any valid suggestion (A1). (g) [2] S in protein only (A1); P in DNA only (A1).

items.answer: antiparallel
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of antiparallel.

items.stem: Define the term "complementary base pairing".
items.answer: The specific pairing of adenine with thymine (or uracil in RNA) and guanine with cytosine by hydrogen bonds

items.stem: Distinguish between the ³⁵S batch in the Hershey–Chase experiment and the ³²P batch.
items.answer: In the ³²P batch the DNA was labelled and most radioactivity was found in the pellet (inside bacteria); in the ³⁵S batch the protein coat was labelled and most radioactivity remained in the supernatant (outside bacteria).

items.stem: Why is the width of the DNA double helix constant along its length?
options: Each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine.
Both strands run in the same direction.
All four bases are the same size.
Hydrogen bonds are all the same length.
items.answer: Each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine.
items.markingKey: A. A purine (two rings) always pairs with a pyrimidine (one ring).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the diversity of possible DNA base sequences is almost limitless.
items.answer: Any of the four bases can occur at each position, with no restriction on order, so a strand of n nucleotides has 4ⁿ possible sequences; even short genes have astronomically many possibilities.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Any of the four bases can occur at each position, with no restriction on order, so a strand of n nucleotides has 4ⁿ possible sequences; even short genes have astronomically many possibilities. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A nucleic acid sample contains 22 % uracil. What can be concluded?
items.answer: The sample is RNA.
items.markingKey: A. Uracil is found only in RNA; single-stranded RNA need not follow Chargaff’s ratios.

items.stem: A student claims: "Hershey and Chase found ³⁵S inside bacteria, proving protein is the genetic material." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most ³⁵S remained outside in the supernatant with the phage coats; ³²P (DNA) entered the bacteria, showing DNA is the genetic material.
items.markingKey: Most ³⁵S remained outside in the supernatant with the phage coats; ³²P (DNA) entered the bacteria, showing DNA is the genetic material. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the bases in DNA are on the inside of the double helix.
items.answer: The bases are relatively hydrophobic and pair by hydrogen bonding with complementary bases; the hydrophilic sugar–phosphate backbone faces the aqueous environment; this also protects the coded information.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The bases are relatively hydrophobic and pair by hydrogen bonding with complementary bases; the hydrophilic sugar–phosphate backbone faces the aqueous environment; this also protects the coded information. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: 3′-GUUGGCCGA-5′; uracil replaces thymine
items.markingKey: Complementary bases with U opposite A (M1); 3′-GUUGGCCGA-5′ (A1); U instead of T (A1).

items.stem: Hana writes: "All RNA molecules are single linear strands with no structure." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: RNA is single-stranded but can fold and base-pair with itself, e.g. tRNA forms a clover-leaf shape and rRNA forms part of ribosome structure.
items.markingKey: RNA is single-stranded but can fold and base-pair with itself, e.g. tRNA forms a clover-leaf shape and rRNA forms part of ribosome structure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analysis of double-stranded DNA from a plasmid from Bacillus shows that 35.4 % of the bases are adenine. Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. Explain why this calculation would not be valid for a single-stranded viral genome.
items.answer: thymine 35.4 %, guanine 14.6 %, cytosine 14.6 %; in single-stranded nucleic acid bases are not paired, so A need not equal T and G need not equal C.
items.markingKey: adenine pairs with thymine so it is also 35.4 % (A1); remaining 29.2 % shared equally by the other pair = 14.6 % each (A1). No complementary strand in a single-stranded genome so Chargaff’s equalities need not hold (R1).

items.stem: One strand of a short DNA molecule has the base sequence 5′-ACAGTATAACGGAGT-3′. Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds holding the two strands together. items.answer: 36 hydrogen bonds; 40 % G–C; higher melting temperature
